newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian internet goes off-line in smut row.
newsitem.headline: Austrian internet goes off-line in smut row.

text.p: Austrian internet access providers pulled the plug on their customers for two hours on Tuesday in protest at what they considered a clumsy attempt by police to clean up the worldwide web.
"Almost 95 percent of all Austrian internet connections were off-line from 4 p.m. (1500 GMT). Almost all firms participated in the strike," said Madeleine Fuchs of internet company Vianet.

The action, sparked by a dawn raid on Vienna-based provider VIPnet, disabled internet connections in most Austrian businesses and many private households. Police impounded VIPnet's entire computer network last week following allegations it had been misused to broadcast child pornography.

The seizure followed a legal complaint filed in Germany in March 1996. The complaint was not against VIPnet but one of its clients who allegedly fed the illegal material into the internet using VIPnet's access points.
"This shockingly incompetent procedure of the authorities should be of concern to all Austrian computer users," the Austrian Association of Internet Providers (ISPA) said.

The association said policemen had disabled VIPnet's computers without shutting them down first, putting the machines at risk of severe damage. By impounding all VIPnet's computers, the authorities had also pushed the firm to the brink of financial ruin, it added.

Austrian police acted against a background of global unease over the darker side of the net. Authorities in Europe and the U.S. have stepped up pressure on providers to weed out unwanted content from cyberspace, so far with only limited success.

In one of the most widely publicised cases, German child pornography investigators searched CompuServe's Munich offices last November and gave the company a list of news groups so hardcore as to be considered illegal.

CompuServe, the country's second-largest internet provider, responded by banning access to some news groups and introducing software to filter out offending pages, drawing severe criticism from free speech advocates.
Austrian authorities have borrowed the German approach, and claim that providers are fully liable for illegal material that is fed into the net through their gateways.

"It is impossible to operate under such conditions," Peter Rastl of ISPA said. "Considering the sheer amount of information that is being made accessible on the net it is neither technically nor practically feasible to control the contents."

"This isn't about kicking off a no-censorship debate or rooting for having criminal content on the internet. What we want from the Austrian authorities is a clear legal basis for providing internet services," he added.

He found support from some Austrian politicians. Peter Kostelka, whip for the ruling Social Democrats, called for new laws to clarify the responsibilities of internet access providers and their customers.
"The Social Democrats are interested in catching those responsible, not punishing the postman," he said.
The justice ministry, meanwhile, conceded that government officials may have been over-zealous in their handling of VIPnet.

Internet providers, who have long maintained their customers should be made responsible for whatever they put on the net, say the real problem is that authorities are still far too ignorant about the risks of cyberspace. ISPA now wants to offer Austrian investigators free computer training and unlimited access to the internet.
"This is a global problem which requires international solutions," Rastl said. "Unfortunately, the internet doesn't stop at borders, but political cooperation does." REUTER
